transcript:
Meeting Header: 2025-04-10 16:00 PDT | Duration: 45m | Attendees: Maya, Ethan, Lena, Samuel, Priya

[00:00] Maya: ok, hey everyone, thanks for carving out time, this is our weekly crestline pilot sync. I'm Maya with Redwood, Ethan's with me from SE. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Lena: hey it's Lena, I have Priya and Sam on from our side.
[00:12] Samuel: Sam here, platform eng.
[00:15] Priya: Priya, product.
[00:17] Ethan: Hi all, Ethan, I'll run through the perf slides and the new micro-benchmarks we pushed this week.

[00:28] Maya: super. Agenda — quick results review, tuning notes, make sure success criteria map to what you need, and then agree on next steps for exec closeout.

[00:40] Ethan: ok so high level, we ran three test profiles: short chat prompts (avg 40 tokens), medium support cases (avg 180 tokens), and long-document summarization tails (avg 1,200 tokens). We exercised our dedicated 2xA100 pilot and the hosted fallback path for overflow.

[01:05] Ethan: numbers — p50 latencies for short were ~85ms, p95 ~170ms, p99 ~290ms on the dedicated pool with batching enabled. For medium, p50 ~210ms, p95 ~420ms, p99 ~780ms. Long tail is where variance goes up — average token throughput held but the p99 hit around 1.8s in a couple of runs.

[01:36] Lena: ok that's useful. The thing we care about is p99 for our SLA for end-user interactive flows — anything above 500ms starts to degrade UX. So the 1.8s spikes are concerning.

[01:50] Ethan: sure, we dug into this. A few contributing factors: 1) sequence length variance causes cache eviction pressure on the KV cache; 2) batching policy — some of the batches were growing to 64 tokens which helps throughput but adds latency for small requests; 3) we didn't have quantization enabled for the long-form model variant in some runs — enabling 4-bit quant reduced memory and lowered stall events in the runtime.

[02:20] Samuel: can you explain the KV cache bit? We heard "K V cash" in an earlier test note and that confused our infra team.

[02:26] Ethan: ha yeah transcription artifact — it's KV cache, key-value cache for past tokens. When you have many long sessions the cache grows and occasionally triggers internal GC-like flows in the runtime, which can spike latencies. Our optimization is to persist prefix cache to memory-mapped files and slide small-session traffic onto a lightweight path.

[02:52] Priya: is that change risky? We need to understand fail-open behavior — if the cache becomes unavailable does latency spike or do requests fallback gracefully?

[03:02] Ethan: good question. The runtime has graceful degradation — if prefix cache misses, we fall back to recomputing contexts which adds cost but keeps latency bounded. We also have an automated fallback to a lower-latency quantized model variant if latency breaches the SLO.

[03:20] Maya: and we showed the tension earlier — you can tune for cost or latency. For Crestline interactive use-case you said latency is more important, right Lena?

[03:28] Lena: yes, interactive flows first. Batch processing we can cost-optimize later.

[03:32] Ethan: so action plan for perf: 1) enable 4-bit quant on the long model in the dedicated cluster, 2) reduce max batch size for interactive route to 8, 3) enable prefix persistence to reduce evictions, and 4) schedule an extended multi-hour run to capture long-tail behavior.

[03:55] Samuel: what's the expected impact? numbers?

[03:58] Ethan: we expect p99 for interactive to drop from ~1.8s to sub-500ms in most runs; for medium flows p99 should move into ~600-700ms range. Throughput per-GPU may fall ~10–15% with smaller batches but net latency SLOs will be satisfied.

[04:20] Priya: ok. On the business side we need the cost model — if throughput drops, what does that do to our unit economics?

[04:27] Maya: we'll update the spreadsheet — I can run two scenarios: latency-first (smaller batches + quant) and cost-first (higher batches, more aggressive caching). We'll show expected cost per 1k requests and monthly spend for your projected volume.

[04:42] Lena: good. Also on compliance: we need SOC 2 artifacts, encryption at rest, and KMS integration details. Who's our contact for that?

[04:50] Maya: that's me — I'll drop the security pack after this call. Ethan has the tech specifics for KMS/HSM integration.

[04:58] Ethan: we support customer-managed keys via KMS, HSM options for on-prem, and audit logs that include token-level routing if you enable extended retention. Note: we redact prompt text in logs unless you opt in for debug.

[05:18] Samuel: retention and residency — the pilot is in our VPC, but we want to ensure data never leaves the region for EU customers. Can Redwood pin instances to region?

[05:28] Ethan: yes — Dedicated pools can be region-pinned. For Private deployments we can do air-gapped on-prem installs if needed. For this pilot we'll ensure nodes are in the same region and we'll enable strict routing.

[05:40] Lena: one practical ask — we saw a few misattributed tokens in the logger where user ids were truncated, could be a parsing bug, can the SE look?

[05:48] Ethan: noted — I'll triage the logging pipeline. That might be downstream of our anonymization layer where we truncate metadata; we'll check the parser.

[05:58] Maya: ok good. Now on closeout — our goal this week is to produce a short exec packet showing that performance meets your success criteria and a pricing ask so your procurement can sign off. Priya, can you share the final success criteria list?

[06:10] Priya: yes. We're aligning internally but top line: interactive p99 < 500ms 95% of the time on production-like load, throughput to sustain 120 QPS with 5 concurrent long sessions, and SOC2 plus KMS proof. Also a commercial cap so monthly cost stays under $X for the pilot — I'll share exact dollar cap after internal sync.

[06:34] Lena: and one more — ability to route degraded sessions to a fallback model with slightly lower accuracy but guaranteed sub-400ms latency.

[06:42] Ethan: we can set a policy-based routing rule for that — e.g., if latency prediction > 350ms, route to low-latency variant.

[06:50] Maya: perfect. Next steps recap — Ethan runs the 12-hour mixed benchmark, Maya sends pricing and security pack, Samuel finalizes VPC access, Priya sends signed success criteria. We'll tentatively schedule an exec wrap for week of Apr 21.

[07:08] Samuel: one more ops question — during benchmark are you going to push with the exact client surface we use (same prompt mix and tokenization)? We want apples-to-apples.

[07:16] Ethan: yes, please upload your canonical prompt seed file to the shared folder; we'll run it unchanged. We'll also seed synthetic long sessions to stress the cache.

[07:24] Priya: do you have a template for the exec packet?

[07:28] Maya: yes — one pager with key metrics, risk items, cost delta, and recommended commercial path. I'll attach it to the action items and mock one up by EOD Friday.

[07:36] Lena: ok thanks. Any blockers?

[07:39] Maya: only the VPC access and Priya's signoff on success criteria.

[07:44] Priya: I can do internal sync tomorrow, will try to get signoff by Tuesday.

[07:48] Ethan: I'll kick off the benchmark tomorrow afternoon after I get the prompt seed and VPC credentials.

[07:52] Maya: great. Quick note on competitors — you asked about Anthropic and SageMaker earlier. Anthropic's managed offering has consistent latency but less tuning surface; SageMaker can be cheaper at scale but requires more ops. We position Redwood as middle ground: high performance with ops-light experience.

[08:10] Lena: understood. We're balancing speed of integration with eventual cost.

[08:14] Maya: ok last thing, I'll capture these as formal action items and I'll share minutes. Thanks everyone, we'll reconvene same time next week unless you prefer exec slot earlier.

[08:25] Priya: same time next week is fine.

[08:28] Maya: thanks all, talk soon.

End of transcript.

Notes: transcript includes occasional minor mishears; timestamps approximate. Shared artifacts referenced: shared benchmarks spreadsheet (link: /drive/crestline/pilot/benchmarks), security pack (link: /drive/crestline/security-pack.pdf), exec packet template (link: /drive/templates/exec-packet.pdf).
